summary: This document defines a MIB subset for energy management of devices. The module covers device identification, context information, and the energy relationships between devices.

eli5.summary: This is a way for devices to say who they are and which other devices power them or are powered by them, so energy use can be tracked.

questions: what is the energy object context mib
what is an energy object in eman
how do energy objects relate to each other
subtitle: A MIB that lets network gear say who it is, how much it matters, and which devices power, meter or aggregate it.

tldr.problem: To manage energy use across network devices, a management system needs to identify each power-using device, know its role, and know how devices relate to each other (who powers whom, who measures whom).
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7461 defines the ENERGY-OBJECT-CONTEXT-MIB with two tables: eoTable for identity, context and links to other MIBs, and eoRelationTable for relationships between Energy Objects. It also defines a small IANA-maintained module for the relationship names.
tldr.outcome: Agents can report identity, importance, role and relationships of Energy Objects over SNMP. It is a Proposed Standard and is a companion to the power monitoring MIB in RFC 7460.

today: RFC 7461 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion for measuring power and energy is RFC 7460.

sections.title: Why an Energy Object Context MIB
sections.content:
RFC 7461 belongs to the Energy Management (EMAN) set of standards. It defines a subset of a Management Information Base (MIB) for energy monitoring of network devices, of devices attached to the network, and possibly of industrial automation devices that have a network interface.

The focus is narrow. The module identifies Energy Objects and reports their context and their relationships, as those ideas are defined in the Energy Management Framework (RFC 7326). Measuring power and energy itself is left to a second module, the Monitoring and Control MIB for Power and Energy (RFC 7460). The scope follows the requirements in RFC 6988.

The document specifies two modules: ENERGY-OBJECT-CONTEXT-MIB and IANA-ENERGY-RELATION-MIB. The second one holds the relationship names so that IANA can add new ones without touching the first.
sections.eli5: This is one half of a toolkit for tracking energy use. This half says who each device is and how devices are connected. The other half counts the energy.

sections.title: Two Tables and the Objects Behind Them
sections.content:
The managed objects live in two tables. eoTable covers identification, context, and links to other MIB modules. eoRelationTable covers the relationships between Energy Objects, in what the RFC calls a simplified representation.

The text groups the objects into five logical parts: identification, context information, links to other MIB modules, relationships, and identity persistence. Identification relies on the ENTITY-MIB (RFC 6933), so each Energy Object is a row there first. As an SNMP MIB, the data is reached through SNMP and written in SMIv2.

Row indexes show how the pieces fit together. A row of eoTable is indexed by entPhysicalIndex. A row of eoRelationTable is indexed by entPhysicalIndex plus an arbitrary eoRelationIndex, so one object can have several relationships.
sections.eli5: There are two lists. One list has a card for every device. The other list says which devices are linked to which, like strings tied between cards.

sections.title: Identification and Context of an Energy Object
sections.content:
Every Energy Object MUST implement entPhysicalIndex, entPhysicalName, entPhysicalClass and entPhysicalUUID from the ENTITY-MIB, and MUST support the entity4CRCompliance level of that MIB. The name must be a printable name. The UUID follows RFC 4122, whose URN form is shown as urn:uuid:f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6.

Each Energy Object MUST belong to exactly one Energy Management Domain, set through the read-write eoDomainName. The domain should map 1:1 with a metered or sub-metered portion of the network. An object acting as a Power Aggregator can only aggregate objects in the same domain.

The context objects describe how the device is used:

  • eoImportance: a rank from 1 (least important) to 100 (most important), default 1. The MIB suggests bands such as 90 to 100 for emergency response and 1 to 39 for decorative or hospitality use.
  • eoKeywords: a comma-separated list of tags for grouping and reporting, up to 2048 octets.
  • eoRoleDescription: free text such as 'Lobby phone'.
  • eoPowerCategory: consumer, producer, meter, distributor or store.
  • eoPowerInterfaceType: inlet, outlet or both.
sections.eli5: Each device gets a name tag with a secret serial number, a team it belongs to, a score from 1 to 100 for how important it is, and a note like 'Lobby phone'.

sections.title: Links to Other MIB Modules
sections.content:
The primary index here is entPhysicalIndex, but a management system must be able to match an Energy Object with its identifiers in other MIBs. If the object is a Power over Ethernet (PoE) port and the Power over Ethernet MIB (RFC 3621) is supported, then eoEthPortIndex and eoEthPortGrpIndex MUST hold the matching pethPsePortIndex and pethPsePortGroupIndex. If the LLDP MIB is supported, eoLldpPortNumber MUST hold the matching lldpLocPortNum. When such a port cannot be specified or is not known, the object is zero.

Optional objects help correlate with other systems: eoMgmtMacAddress, eoMgmtAddressType, eoMgmtAddress, eoMgmtDNSName, and the text key eoAlternateKey. An optional object that an implementation does not include should answer with noSuchInstance when polled. The text also notes that identity information may be worth persisting across a device reload, for example for PoE phones on a switch, but of little use for mobile user PCs on a wireless access point.
sections.eli5: A device may already have a name in other lists, like a port number on a switch. This MIB copies those names so a person can match the same device across lists.

sections.title: Energy Object Relationships
sections.content:
A row in eoRelationTable links one Energy Object, given by its entPhysicalIndex, to a remote Energy Object, given by its UUID in eoRelationID. The UUID MUST comply with RFC 4122. An Energy Object may have no relationships at all.

Three kinds of relationship are defined, each with two directions: metering (meteredBy and metering), power source (poweredBy and powering) and aggregation (aggregatedBy and aggregating). If B is poweredBy A, then A is powering B. The value is stored in eoRelationship, and the row is managed with eoRelationStatus and eoRelationStorageType (default nonVolatile).

Preferably, eoRelationID uses the entPhysicalUUID of the other object. If the UUID is unknown or nonexistent, it is a zero-length string.
sections.eli5: It is like a family tree for devices: this lamp is plugged into that outlet, and that meter measures this lamp. Each fact can be read from either side.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Several objects are read-write or read-create. Unauthorized changes to eoDomainName, entPhysicalName, eoRoleDescription, eoKeywords, eoImportance, eoAlternateKey or the relationship objects MAY disrupt power and energy collection, and therefore any predefined policies in the network.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features, and those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy with the User-based Security Model and the AES cipher. Operators must make sure only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects.

The RFC also warns that energy and power monitoring can reveal sensitive information about individuals' activities and habits, so monitoring of individuals and homes should happen only with proper authorization.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could change the name tags, the energy reports would get muddled. So only trusted people should be allowed to change them, and nobody should spy on how a family uses power.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The Energy Object Context module is recorded in the SMI Numbers registry as energyObjectContextMIB at { mib-2 231 }. The document also defines the first version of the IANA-maintained IANA-ENERGY-RELATION-MIB, recorded as ianaEnergyRelationMIB at { mib-2 232 }.

Any change to the energy relationships requires Specification Required, as defined in RFC 5226. Keeping the names in a separate IANA module is what lets new relationships be added without revising the main module.
sections.eli5: The official number registry gives these two lists their own spots. If someone wants a new kind of link between devices, they need a written description first.

items.label: poweredBy
items.desc: Object A is powered by object B.

items.label: powering

items.label: meteredBy

items.label: aggregatedBy
items.desc: Object A is aggregated by object B.

items.label: aggregating
items.desc: Object A is aggregating object B.
